Hi Lara,

I’m sorry I didn’t have a chance to respond to your Teams message on Thursday – It was a packed day and I’ve been trying to manage the water project with a lot of changes lately.

First, thank you for working on the IRWM contact list, I will be presetting to the RAC this Wednesday, and it will be helpful to continue working with that group as things are moving fast.

The project has been a bit overwhelming, and we are working on a tight timeline to make the April 26th Water Assembly kick-off event come together. One thing that I brought up to Crystal and Stephanie is that we will need a speaker during this program to cover a technical piece concerning the drought status (UCSD was originally scoped for this work but has too much to cover with the literature review). I would like to check in with you to see if you may have any contacts who could fill this role and present a 10-15 minute presentation on April 26th? We would need all material/PPTs ready by April 14th, so I know this is a big ask.

Additionally, if you do not have any contacts, UCSD recommended these potential presenters:

  1.  Jeffrey Mount<https://www.ppic.org/person/jeffrey-mount/>, Public Policy Institute of California (first choice)

He could speak to the drought in terms of long-term trends, provide context for this year, and discuss what is on the horizon, first from a State perspective, but also identifying challenges specific to the RWER region.

  1.  Dr. F. Martin Ralph<https://mralph.scrippsprofiles.ucsd.edu/>, Director, Center for Western Weather Extremes<https://cw3e.ucsd.edu/>, Scripps Institute of Oceanography
Local technical expert on the physical process related to extremes in precipitation, climate projections, etc.

  1.  Luca Delle Monache<https://ldellemonache.scrippsprofiles.ucsd.edu/>, Deputy Director, Center for Western Weather Extremes, Scripps Institute of Oceanography
  2.  Tom Corringham, Research Economist, Center for Western Weather Extremes<https://cw3e.ucsd.edu/>, Scripps Institute of Oceanography

If you have time to secure a person either from this list or from your own recommendation, it would be really helpful to have your support with this task. I have mentioned this to Crystal and Stephanie, so if anyone can secure a presenter let’s keep each other posted.

Please feel free to give me a call this week if that’s easier, and thanks for all your effort on this project!

Hi Joel,

Thanks again for your participation in the interview for this project.  We do have a couple follow up questions we’d like your input on below.  These are not meant to take more than 10-15 minutes of your time and it would greatly benefit our analysis.  Also, when able, we’d definitely be interested in viewing the maps you mentioned showing historic and current extents of agriculture, as well as ideal lands to increase agriculture throughout the region.

	a.	What do you see as the biggest risk(s) to the San Diego and Imperial region’s water supply portfolio with respect to long-term resilience?

Cost - heavy regional infrastructure investment creates a burden on consumers that they may not be able to support for uses that do not benefit them. Solutions need to be localized to individual communities to ensure resident buy-in and ability to pay. Communities need to be engaged to create community-specific drought resilience plans to prepare for reduced allocations at a neighborhood-level during drought conditions. To ease this burden, non-essential irrigation and consumptions should be eliminated and/or disincentivized with a heavily graduated pay scale based on per-capita volume for residential and commercial customers. This will incentivize further conservation, allowing for existing water supplies to be allocated more equitably. As an essential service for local residents, agricultural allocations should receive priority up to 1/3 of the regional allocation at special rates, so long as these farms contribute to the local food supply. We must prioritize use of precious water resources for urban greening in low-income neighborhoods and for agricultural production for local consumption in order to ensure regional resilience during drought conditions.

	a.	Can you identify the top three water management projects types/solutions that you’d recommend the San Diego and Imperial region allocate more funding/effort towards?

                                                         i.      Regional Water Recycling

                                                       ii.      Localized On-Site Reuse (Graywater) - First, see below.

                                                     iii.      Stormwater Capture and Reuse/Recycling

                                                     iv.      Desalination - Third; costly but reliable source during drought conditions depending on energy availability

                                                       v.      Storage Management - Increase Dam Capacity

                                                     vi.      Storage Management - Manage Groundwater Recharge

                                                   vii.      Conservation - Second; eliminate non-essential consumption to alleviate water budget.

	a.	Which of the following water supply solutions do you view at the “most at risk” in terms of being a reliable, long term source of water for the region? Which is “least at risk”?  Write “most risk” and “least risk” after two of the options below, and elaborate in 1-2 sentences on why.

                                                         i.      Regional Water Recycling

                                                       ii.      Localized On-Site Reuse (Graywater) - Least Risk

                                                     iii.      Stormwater Capture and Reuse/Recycling

                                                     iv.      Desalination

                                                       v.      Storage Management - Increase Dam Capacity

                                                     vi.      Storage Management - Manage Groundwater Recharge - Most Risk

                                                   vii.      Conservation

Least risk - Graywater use effectively eliminates the need for landscape irrigation, which is responsible for roughly half of urban water consumption. This is one of the most effective forms of conservation with the most co-benefits. In terms of resilience, localized systems such as graywater application are more effective at using water with less maintenance costs than largescale regional infrastructure.

Greatest risk - extraction from groundwater basins must be monitored and regulated based on recharge rates in order to avoid depletion. For this reason, groundwater basins are not currently relied upon for urban areas. However, aquifer levels should be monitored and managed in areas which are adding new residential developments, ex: San Pasqual Valley.

Thank you,

Subject: Announcement: Welcome Bethany Facendini, OSEJ GPM Community Engagement

Greetings All,

I am thrilled to introduce Bethany Facendini, our new Community Engagement and Outreach Manager for the Office of Sustainability and Environmental Justice (OSEJ). Bethany is an experienced community organizer and sustainability advocate, and she will lead our efforts to engage and empower diverse communities throughout our region for climate action.

Bethany will develop and implement strategies to foster community connections and participation in environmental justice and sustainability initiatives. She will work closely with community benefit organizations, leaders, practitioners, and residents to create opportunities for collaboration and partnership.

Bethany brings a wealth of experience and expertise to OSEJ, including numerous community engagement roles in the San Francisco Bay Area and beyond, most recently with Sonoma County Regional Parks as the Community Engagement Division Manager. There, she directed marketing, communications, and cross-sector partnerships, as well as created sustainability and equity-based programs for diverse audiences, community needs assessments, and evaluation systems. In addition, Bethany helped increase the number of culturally relevant programs for under-represented populations (BIPOC, youth impacted by systems, people with disabilities, and families with low incomes). She also served as Sonoma County Human Services’ Community Engagement Manager where she led community programs to increase awareness of services and community outreach events; cultivated relationships between private, governmental, and non-profit organizations to improve partnerships; and built community networks to connect marginalized groups to programs and services. From 2013 – 2015 as the Community Engagement Coordinator for the Sonoma County Department of Health Services, Bethany worked on community engagement and outreach to advance health equity systems change initiatives. She has a Master of Arts in Environmental and Social Justice and a Bachelor of Arts degree in English and LGBTQ Studies. She also has an Urban Environmental Education Certification from Cornell University.

Bethany has world travel and living abroad experience in 46 countries, mostly economically developing nations, and recently returned from a year-long sabbatical traveling solo around the world.

We are excited to have Bethany on board and look forward to her leadership in advancing our environmental justice and sustainability goals. Please join me in welcoming Bethany to our team.

Enjoy the day,

eden

Eden Brukman, Chief Sustainability Officer
